scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The rigaudon originated as a lively 17th-century folk dance in southern France, especially Provence, Dauphiné, Vivarais, and Languedoc.
It was danced by couples with hopping steps and a duple meter.
Madame de Sévigné noted it in 1672 as popular among all social classes.
on_screen: Map: France · Europe
Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The rigaudon was danced at court balls in the 17th and 18th centuries and at village festivals, weddings, and social gatherings in Provence and Dauphiné.
It marked celebrations and communal joy, embodying merriment and spirited social interaction.
Its popularity spanned social classes, from peasants to aristocrats.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Rigaudon music is in lively duple or cut time (2/2), often with regular eight-measure phrases and a quarter-note upbeat.
The rhythm features steady quarter and eighth notes creating a hopping feel.
Listen for the harpsichord, strings, woodwinds, baroque orchestra.
The pulse is duple meter, typically 2/2 or 2/4.
Bright harpsichord or string textures with a steady, hopping rhythm in duple meter; phrases are regular and balanced, evoking cheerful, lively courtly dance.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Madame de Sévigné noted the rigaudon in 1672 as a popular dance.
The dancing master Rigaud is reputed as its inventor.
The rigaudon has regional variants in Provence and Dauphiné, with the latter adapting the dance to mountain culture.
The rigaudon descends from French folk dances of the 17th century and influenced baroque court dances.
on_screen: Names on screen as they are spoken
Variant names as a small list

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Rigaudon is sibling of bourrée: Shares similar duple meter and hopping rhythm but rigaudon is rhythmically simpler.
Rigaudon is related folk dance of farandole: Another lively Provençal folk dance, often performed in circle.
Rigaudon is sibling of passepied: Baroque dance that, like rigaudon, declined in ballroom popularity by late 18th century.
Rigaudon is related folk and baroque dance of gigue: Also a lively dance in compound meter, part of baroque suites.
